# The story, chapter by chapter

> **Spoilers.** This page reveals the story as it unfolds through the year. Read the world and district pages first if you want to discover it in the game.

The story is told in a prologue, twelve chapters (one per district, opened by passing its gate) and an epilogue for the Year of Keeping.

## Prologue: The Morning After the Tide

*Find the Archive*

You smelled the sea long before you saw it. For three days the coast road had climbed and dipped through heather and gorse, under a sky the colour of wet slate, and for three days you had walked it without being entirely sure why. You had a pack, a stick of blackthorn, a little bread, and a feeling, low and steady as a heartbeat, that you were expected somewhere. On the fourth morning the road crested the Ammerhold, and there, below you, was Veyra.

It is built into the seaward face of the ridge, tier upon tier, like a great stair cut by giants and then forgotten. Roofs of grey slate and green copper climb from the harbour to the heights. Bridges leap between the tiers. Towers lean companionably together. Far below, the river Lethe slides out of a gorge and loses itself in the Grey Sea, and over all of it, over the roofs and the water and the steps, lay a thin silver haze, lifting slowly in the morning sun, the way breath lifts from a horse in winter.

The city gate stood open and unguarded. Inside, people moved about their business in a strange, slow way, as if they had all woken at once from the same long dream. A baker stood in his doorway holding a tray of loaves and frowning at them, as if he could not think why he had made so many. A woman walked up the street calling for her dog by three different names, one after another, and looked more frightened each time. Two old men sat on a bench arguing gently about whether they were brothers.

Nobody stopped you. Nobody seemed to notice you at all. You climbed, because climbing felt right, up stairs worn hollow by nine hundred years of feet, past shuttered shops and silent fountains, until at the very top of the city you came to a round hall of pale stone under a dome of green copper, and a pair of great bronze doors standing a little open. Above them, in letters nearly worn away, someone long ago had carved: WHAT IS PLACED IS KEPT.

Inside it was cool and dim and smelled of dust and lamp oil. Shelves climbed in rings to the roof, crowded with tall leather books. In the middle of the floor stood a great brass bowl on a pillar of black stone, cold and dark. And at the foot of the pillar, surrounded by a snowdrift of small white paper cards, sat a young woman in a long brown coat, turning the pages of a ledger very slowly, as if she hoped they might change their minds. Every page was blank.

She looked up when your shadow fell across the cards. "Oh! Sorry. Mind your feet. No, not that one, that's Tuesday." She scooped a handful of cards out of your way and stood up, all elbows and ink-stained fingers. "I'm Wren. Wren Halloway. I work here. I'm the junior archivist, which as of this morning means I'm the only archivist, which as of this morning doesn't mean very much." She looked at you properly then, and something in her face changed. "You're not from the city, are you? You've still got all your edges."

She told you about the Tide while you helped her gather the cards. How it rises off the river every evening like mist off a bath. How it takes whatever you're not holding tight. How last night it had come up thicker than anyone alive had ever seen it, thick as fleece, and how this morning half the city couldn't remember the other half. "And the Archivist is gone," she said. "Calder. She was here when I left last night and this morning she just... isn't. Her coat's on the hook. Her tea's on the desk, cold. And every ledger in this building has been wiped clean. Nine hundred years of the city's memory, and it's just paper now."

She was quiet for a moment. Then she went to the desk and came back holding a brass lantern, old and dented, with a little door of smoked glass. "This was on her chair," she said. "Only thing she left. There's an old saying, that a Warden's lamp lights for whoever truly remembers. I've tried it. I've tried it forty times this morning." She laughed, not very happily. "It doesn't light for paper, apparently, and paper is all I've got." She held it out. "Go on. You might as well. Everybody else has."

The lantern was cold as a stone from a stream. You held it, feeling foolish. And then, deep inside the smoked glass, something stirred: not a flame exactly, but a faint warmth, the colour of honey, the size of a grain of barley. It flickered and nearly died, and flickered again, and held.

Wren stared at it. Then she stared at you. "Well," she said at last, very softly. "Well, that's not supposed to happen." High above you, in the gallery that ran around the dome, a door closed with a quiet click. When you both looked up, there was nobody there, only a little drift of silver mist hanging in the air where someone had just been standing.

Wren let out a long breath. "Right," she said. "I think you'd better stay. I think you'd better learn how to keep that thing lit. And I think," she added, picking up a single notecard from the floor and turning it over in her fingers, "I'd better learn with you." Far below, the Lethe murmured to itself in its gorge, and the morning mist went on rising off the roofs of Veyra, slowly, patiently, as if it had all the time in the world.

## Chapter One: The Lamps of the Quay

*Relight the lamps along Lamplighters' Quay*

Lamplighters' Quay runs along the river where it widens before the sea: a long curve of black stone wharves, crooked warehouses and tall iron lamp-posts, forty-four of them, each crowned with a glass lantern the size of a barrel. For six hundred years a Warden lit them every dusk, and the Tide that rose from the water broke around their light like a stream around stones. For three hundred years they had stood dark. In the weeks since you came, you and Wren have lit them again, one by one, every evening, a little further each night.

It is not done with flint and oil. You stand beneath each post and do what you have been practising: you take the things the Quay folk bring you, a list of debts, a child's name, the order of a fisherman's nets, and you turn each one into a picture so vivid and so strange that it could not possibly be forgotten. A debt becomes a gull wearing a ledger like a hat. A child named Pell becomes a bell the size of a barn. When you hold them all at once, clear and bright, the lantern in your hand grows warm, and the great lamp above you catches, and blooms, and the Quay folk cheer.

Old Tansy watches from her stall under the last lamp, where she sells rosemary tea "for the remembering" and gives advice that nobody has asked for. "You're holding the cup wrong," she told you on your first night. "And you're thinking too hard. A memory's not a thing you grip. It's a thing you put somewhere." She would not say where she had learned that. She has a way of looking at you, over the rim of her teacup, as if you remind her of someone she cannot quite place.

On the twelfth night, the lamps began going out again. You found them in the morning, cold, their glass fogged on the inside with a thin silver bloom. On the fifteenth night, Wren saw who was doing it: three figures in long hooded robes the colour of river mist, moving softly along the Quay after midnight, pausing beneath each lamp just long enough to breathe on the glass. "Hushed," Mosk the ferryman said, and spat into the river. "The Quiet Order. They say they're doing us a kindness."

You waited for them on the twentieth night, under the last lamp, with Wren beside you holding a cudgel she plainly had no idea how to use. They came out of the mist without a sound. The tallest of them stopped a few paces away and lowered his hood, and he was only a young man, pale and gentle-faced, with eyes that looked very tired. "Let it go, friend," he said, kindly. "Whatever you are holding on to. It only hurts. The river would take it from you so gently, if you'd let it."

You did not let it go. You held the whole Quay in your mind instead: forty-four lamps, forty-four pictures, each one in its place along the water, and the lantern in your hand blazed up so bright that the young man flinched and turned his face away, and the mist around the Hushed thinned and drew back like a dog that has been shouted at. When you could see again, they were gone. Only a single grey glove lay on the wet stones, finely made, with a closed eye stitched in silver thread on the cuff.

Under the base of the last lamp, where the iron had rusted through, Wren found a fold of paper wrapped in oilcloth. It was in Calder's small, fierce handwriting, and the ink was not quite a week old. Hold it as a picture or not at all, it said. Words drift. Pictures anchor. Places hold. If you are reading this, you have found the first. There are eleven more. Trust no one who offers you peace.

Wren read it three times. Then she took a single notecard from her coat, looked at it for a long moment, and tore it in half and dropped the pieces into the river. "Practice," she said, not quite steadily, and would not tell you what had been written on it. Behind you, along the whole long curve of the Quay, the lamps burned gold against the dark, and for the first time in three hundred years the Tide rose that night and went back down again without taking anything at all.

## Chapter Two: The Walk of Portraits

*Walk Calder's route through the Long Gallery*

The Long Gallery runs for almost a mile through the heart of the second tier: a single vaulted corridor of honey-coloured stone, lit by high round windows, its walls hung with portraits from floor to ceiling. Every Warden, every Archivist, every Harbour Mistress and Guildmaster and hero of Veyra for nine centuries looked down from those walls. On the morning after the great Tide, every one of them was blank. Nine hundred years of faces, gone to bare canvas and gilt frames.

The caretaker, an old man named Fennick with a voice like a creaking door, showed you the worn path down the middle of the floor. "She walked it every night," he said. "The Archivist. Thirty-one years, never missed. In at the east door at nine, out at the west door at ten. Never looked left nor right. Just walked, with her lips moving." He shook his head. "I asked her once what she was saying. She said, 'I'm visiting.'"

So you walked it too. Each night you built your own palace alongside Calder's: your own route, through a place you know with your eyes shut, and at each stop you set a picture and made it do something to the place. And as your route grew longer and surer, a strange thing happened in the Gallery. The portraits began, one by one, to come back. First a smudge of colour. Then a pair of eyes. Then a whole face, stern or smiling, looking down at you as you passed as if it had only just stepped back into its frame.

Wren read the little brass plates beneath them aloud as the faces returned. "Ysolde of the Lamp. Corvin the Mason, who laid out the Quay. Annet Gale, who held the Gate alone for a whole night in the Year of Floods." She was quiet for a while. "I never knew who any of them were. Not really. They were just pictures I walked past on my way to work." She looked at you sideways. "Is it wrong that I'm a bit jealous of the paintings? They get to remember who they are."

On the twenty-fourth night the Hushed came to the Gallery. You heard them before you saw them, a soft shuffle of many feet at both ends of the corridor, and then the high windows began, one after another, to fog over with silver from the outside. In a minute the Gallery was dark as the inside of a fist. Somewhere ahead a voice said, quite calmly, "Search the frames. She hid something here. The Grand Hush wants it before the moon turns." Wren's hand found yours in the dark and held on hard enough to hurt.

There was no light to see by. There was only your route. You stood still and walked it in your mind, every stop, every picture, and then you walked it backwards, from the last stop to the first, and your feet followed in the dark, thirty paces, a turn, eighteen paces, the cold stone pillar on your left exactly where the picture said it would be. You led Wren out through a side door that Fennick had shown you on your first night, while behind you the Hushed searched an empty hall by the light of their own silver mist.

In the morning you went back. Behind the frame of Annet Gale, in a narrow gap between canvas and stone, was a second page in Calder's hand. The city is a palace, it said. I built it to be walked. I walked it every night so that I would never be the only one who knew the way. If you are reading this, walk it further than I did. And at the bottom, in smaller writing, as if added in haste: The courier knows the road. Keep the courier safe.

"Courier," Wren said. "What courier?" You did not know. But that night, falling asleep, you dreamed of a road at night, and rain, and an old woman's voice saying, very close to your ear, "Again. From the beginning. Again," and you woke with your heart pounding and the lantern on the table beside your bed glowing gold all by itself.

## Chapter Three: The Faces in the Stone

*Restore the Hall of Faces and learn who walks behind the Hushed*

The Hall of Faces is a round chamber deep in the third tier, with no windows at all. Its walls are carved from top to bottom with the faces of every Keeper the Archive ever trained, each one cut into the living rock by its owner's own hand on the day they swore the Compact. The Tide cannot reach into stone. But on the morning after the great Tide, the names beneath the faces were gone, and without the names, the faces were only strangers in the dark.

You gave them back their names. That is what this month has been: learning to look at a face, choose the one thing about it that will not change, and fasten a name to it with a picture so firmly that it will never come loose. Wren held the lamp while you worked. By the end of the month there were three hundred and twelve names cut fresh beneath three hundred and twelve faces, and one face, low on the eastern wall, that nobody could name, because someone had taken a chisel to it and scratched it into a ruin.

Wren would not look at it. "It gives me a headache," she said, and laughed, and went to sit by the door. Every time you passed it, you felt her not looking at it.

It was on the walk home from the Hall that you met Joss Hask. More exactly, you met three Salt Guild bullies who were explaining to a fish-seller in a quiet alley that she would be buying a cup of the grey from them every week from now on, and then, a few seconds later, you met Joss Hask, who came out of a doorway behind them like a door coming off its hinges. He was the largest man you had ever seen. He did not shout. He did not seem to hurry. When it was over, the three of them were sitting in the gutter looking puzzled about how they had got there, and Hask was handing the fish-seller her basket back.

"Road-warden," he said, when you asked. "Out of Kettering Ford." He looked at your lantern, then at your face, for rather a long time. "Looking for some men." He did not say which men, and you did not ask, and he walked back with you to the Archive as if that had always been the plan. Wren took one look at him and said, "Oh good. A wall that walks," and he very nearly smiled.

Two nights later, on the Quay, you met the Grand Hush. He was standing behind a trestle table in a grey hood, ladling soup into bowls for a long line of the hungry and the half-forgotten, and he looked up as you passed and smiled at you, and it was the kindest smile you have ever seen. "the Keeper," he said. You had never told anyone in the Order your name. "I am so glad to meet you at last. You must be very tired. Carrying things always makes us tired."

He came round the table and took your hand in both of his. His hands were warm and dry, and smelled faintly of rosemary and rain. "I want you to know," he said quietly, "that whatever she gave you, you are allowed to put it down. No one will blame you. I won't. I know how heavy it is. I carried something once, for years, and the day I let it go was the first day of my life." Behind you, Hask had gone very still. The Grand Hush let go of your hand, and bowed, and went back to his soup.

That night Wren sat up late with the scratched face. You found her there at midnight, with the lamp, running her fingers over the broken stone. "It's a woman," she said, without turning round. "Young. About my age. Someone hated her very much, to do this." She was quiet. "Or loved her very much. I can't tell which." The third page of Calder's ledger was tucked behind the little bronze lamp-hook beside it. It said only: Forgive me. It was the only way to hide you.

## Chapter Four: The Ledger of Debts

*Crack the number code of the Counting House*

The Counting House stands on the fourth tier above the harbour, a tall, narrow building of black timber and small leaded windows, where for six hundred years every coin that came into Veyra was counted and recorded. Its ledgers did not go blank in the Tide. They did not need to. They had always been written in a number code that nobody alive could read, and Calder had kept every one of them, and she had written in their margins in the same code, in her own hand.

The code turned out to be the old Wardens' sound-cipher, the one you spent this month learning: each digit a sound, each pair of digits a word, each word a picture. Ninety-four is a bear. Seventy-four is a car. Once you could see the pictures, the numbers stopped being numbers and became a story, and the story was a very ugly one. Hask sat beside you through the long evenings, saying nothing, and reading over your shoulder with his lips moving.

The story went like this. Every month for nine years, the Salt Guild had paid a great sum into an account marked only with a closed eye. Every month, a smaller sum had gone out of that same account, to a long list of names. Some of the names were Guild men. Some were officers of the Watch. Three were clerks of the Archive. And one, from the very last year, was a clerk of the Counting House named Ollery, who had not been seen since the night of the great Tide.

You found Ollery in a rooming house by the salt pans, sitting by a cold grate, perfectly content. He did not know his name. He did not know what year it was. He offered you tea and then forgot he had offered it, and offered it again. On the table by his chair was an empty glass vial with a silver bloom inside it, and a slip of paper with a closed eye drawn on it, and the words: With the gratitude of the Order. Be at peace.

Hask stood in the doorway for a long time looking at the old clerk. "My brother," he said at last, "looks like that now." It was the most he had said about himself in a month. On the walk back he told you the rest: about Tomas, and the marsh-houses, and the month of searching, and the smile. "I keep their names in my head," he said, meaning the Guild men. "Paper gets found." You understood then why he had looked so long at your lantern on the night you met.

The last page of Calder's margins was the strangest. It was a sum, a long column of figures, and she had not finished it. The total line was empty. Wren stared at it until her eyes watered. It was you who saw it, finally, because the figures were not a sum at all; they were a date, written as pictures: a sail, a lion, a cage, a bell. The twenty-first of Deepwinter. "That's the longest night of the year," Wren said slowly. And then, going white: "That's the Night of No Moon."

You found the fourth page of the ledger folded inside the spine of the book. Count what they take, it read, and you will know what they want. They do not want money. Money is only what they use. Watch the clocks.

## Chapter Five: The Clockmaker's Warning

*Restart the clocks of the Clockwork Market and read the schedule of the Tide*

Every one of the hundred and twelve clocks in the Clockwork Market stopped on the night of the great Tide, at nine minutes past eleven. They are not ordinary clocks. They were built by the Wardens to keep the timetable of the river: when the Tide would rise, how thick, how high, for every night of a nineteen-year cycle. Wound and set, they told the whole city when to light its lamps. Stopped, they told nobody anything.

Restarting them was like this month's training: long strings of numbers, set to pictures, laid along a route through the market, each stall a stop, each clock a pair of images. As each clock started to tick again, the market woke around you. Stall-keepers who had sat for weeks in a daze began to call out prices. Children chased each other between the gears. And the great clock in the market tower, the Mother Clock, began, very slowly, to move its iron hands toward a date marked on its face in red: the Night of No Moon.

It was while you were up on the scaffold beside the Mother Clock, with your hands deep in its brass innards, that someone tried to kill you. You did not see him. You only heard the flat crack of a crossbow from the gallery opposite, and felt the bolt go past your ear close enough to stir your hair, and then a second crack, and a grunt, and the sound of something heavy falling a long way onto cobbles. When you looked down, there was a man in a grey hood lying very still in the square, and a woman standing over him, lowering a small silver crossbow of her own.

She looked up at you and smiled. She was dark-haired and dark-eyed and dressed in green velvet that probably cost more than the Counting House, and she was not even slightly out of breath. "Isolde Varre," she called up. "Harbour Mistress. You're welcome. Do come to dinner on Thursday. Bring the large one, he looks fun." She stepped over the dead man as if he were a puddle, and was gone into the crowd before you had reached the bottom of the ladder.

Varre House was all candlelight and black marble and card tables. Isolde played three hands of Rook against Hask and won all three, and then sent the servants away and told you about the Grand Hush. "His name is Sevrin Ashgrave," she said, shuffling. "Twelve years ago he had a wife called Marra and a little girl called Lia, and the Red Fever took them both in one week. He drank a cup of the grey the night they were buried. He says it was the first night he ever slept." She dealt. "Since then he has been trying to give everyone else the same good night's sleep."

"Why are you telling us this?" Wren asked. Isolde looked at her for a long moment over her cards. "Because the clocks are running again, which means you've seen the date. And because I would very much like there to still be a city on the twenty-second of Deepwinter, for purely selfish reasons. I own most of it." She smiled. "Also, someone tried to kill one of my favourite new acquaintances in my favourite market. I take that personally."

The fifth page of Calder's ledger was not hidden at all. It was waiting for you on your pillow when you came back to the Archive that night, though the doors had been locked and Wren swore nobody had been in. It said: They will try to frighten you, then flatter you, then buy you. When none of that works, they will try to make the city hate you. Do not let it make you hate the city.

## Chapter Six: What the Bridge Remembers

*Read the inscriptions on the Tongues Bridge*

The Tongues Bridge crosses the Lethe gorge in a single high arch of white stone, so old and so slender that it looks as if it ought to fall down and has simply never got round to it. Every block of it is carved with words in the old tongue of the Wardens, a language nobody has spoken in five hundred years: the Compact, the laws of the city, the names of the floods. The Tide has no power over carved stone. The words were all still there. It was only that nobody could read them.

So you learned to. A word at a time, a sound-picture at a time, the way you learn any foreign tongue: find something it sounds like, make it do something to what it means, then test yourself on it tomorrow and next week and next month until it is yours. Wren learned with you, and Hask, and even Isolde sent a note that said, Teach me the rude ones. By the end of the month you could walk the whole bridge and read it aloud from end to end, and the old words rang in the gorge like bells.

Halfway across, on the downstream parapet, there was one inscription that was new. It had been carved within the year, quickly, in a hand you knew at once. It recorded, in the old tongue and in the formal manner of the Wardens, that on the night of the great Tide the Lethe Gate had been opened a hand's width from the inside, with the Archivist's own key, by the Archivist's own hand. It was signed: E. Calder.

Wren read it four times. Then she sat down on the stones with her back against the parapet and put her face in her hands. "She did it," she said, through her fingers. "She let it in. All of it. The ledgers, the names, my... Everything that was lost that night. She let it in." Hask stood over her like a wall against the wind. Nobody said anything for a long time. Below you the Lethe ran grey and fast and quiet through its gorge.

By the next morning, the Hushed had painted it on every wall in Veyra. THE ARCHIVIST BETRAYED YOU, in tall grey letters on the Quay, on the market tower, on the doors of the Counting House, on the bronze doors of the Archive itself. Beneath each one, in smaller letters: The Order forgives her. Will you? People stood in front of them in silent knots, reading, and when you walked past with your lantern, they turned and watched you go, and their faces were not friendly.

That evening, at the foot of the Archive steps, someone threw a stone. It struck Wren on the temple and she went down on one knee. Hask had the man by the collar before he had finished throwing it, and then stopped, because it was only Mosk the ferryman, weeping, saying over and over, "She took my wife's name. She took my wife's name. I can't remember my wife's name." Wren got up, blood running down into her eye, and took the old man's hands, and said, "I know. I know. I'm so sorry. I can't remember my mother's face."

The sixth page of the ledger was found by Isolde, of all people, sewn into the lining of a Hushed robe her men had taken off a smuggler. It was the shortest so far. They will tell you I opened the gate, it said. I did. Ask them why, and watch what they say. Then ask the Scriptorium.

## Chapter Seven: The Two Chronicles

*Discover the true account of the night of the great Tide*

The Scriptorium is a cold, quiet maze of reading rooms beneath the fifth tier, where for centuries the clerks of the Archive copied out the Ledgers by hand so that there would always be a spare. Most of its copies went blank in the Tide like everything else. But the Quiet Order, it turned out, had its own scriptorium, and its own copyists, and within a week of the painting on the walls there were two accounts of the night of the great Tide being passed from hand to hand in every tavern in Veyra.

They told the same story, very nearly. The Archivist had gone to the Lethe Gate after midnight with her key. She had opened the sluice a hand's width. The Tide had come up through the city thick as wool. In the morning, she was gone. The difference was in the small things: in times, in names, in who was where. One said she had gone alone. The other said she had been seen with a stranger, a traveller in a road-cloak. One said she had laughed. The other said she had wept.

This month's work was to take the two accounts apart, fact by fact, and set each fact in its own place, and look at the shape they made. It is slow, patient work, the kind Calder must have done every day of her life. You built a palace for each chronicle and walked them side by side, and where they disagreed, you marked the stop. By the end of the month you had forty-one marks. And you had noticed something else: every one of the forty-one differences made Calder look worse.

Then Brother Ennick came to the Archive door in the rain. He was a young acolyte of the Order, freckled and thin, and he was shaking so badly he could barely stand. He had a copy of the Order's own private record of that night, stolen from the Grand Hush's study, wrapped in his robe against his skin. "I copied it myself," he said. "Three years ago they put me on copying. I joined them to forget my father. And then I started noticing that we were writing things down. All of us. All the time. An order that preaches forgetting, keeping more records than the Archive." His teeth chattered. "That's when I started remembering how to be frightened."

The Order's own record told it straight. On the night of the great Tide, nine Hushed agents had been inside the Archive, working with three bribed clerks, searching for something they called the Heart. Calder had found them there. She could not fight nine men. So she went to the Gate and opened it a hand's width, just enough, and the Tide came up through the city and through the Archive and took from the nine agents every memory of what they had come to find. It took the ledgers too. She had known it would. She chose it anyway.

And there was one more line, underlined by the Grand Hush himself: The Heart is not in the building. The Archivist has put it in a living ledger. Find the courier.

Wren read it by candlelight with her hand pressed flat against the bandage on her temple. When she had finished she sat very still. Then she said, in a small voice, "She didn't betray us. She burned the house down to keep the thief from the cradle." She laughed shakily. "That's much worse, somehow. That's much more like her." The seventh page of Calder's ledger had been in Ennick's bundle all along, and he had never noticed. It said: Now you know why. Do not forgive me yet. You do not know the price.

## Chapter Eight: The Race of the Evening Tide

*Climb the Tidal Stair before the Tide*

The Tidal Stair climbs the full height of Veyra in one long, steep, winding flight: one thousand and eleven steps from the harbour to the Archive, cut into the cliff, with the sea on one side and the city on the other. Every evening the Tide floods up it from the river like water up a drainpipe, and every evening for nine hundred years, children have raced it from bottom to top for a dare. This month you raced it too, every evening, with a list in your head that grew longer each night, because a mind that is fast and sure is a mind the Tide cannot catch.

On the twenty-sixth evening, the Hushed came for you on the Stair. They came up from below and down from above at once, a dozen of them, silent in their mist-grey robes, and the Tide was already rising behind them like a white wall. Wren was beside you. Hask was twenty steps behind, fighting three of them at once on a landing barely wide enough for one. "Go!" he roared, which was the first time you had ever heard him raise his voice. "Go, I'll be along!"

You ran. You ran with the whole palace in your head, every name, every number, every face, and the Tide coming up behind you cold as a cellar, and the lantern burning so bright in your fist that the Hushed ahead of you fell back from it, shielding their eyes. Four hundred steps. Six hundred. Wren was gasping and laughing at once. "I hate stairs," she panted. "I have always hated stairs. When this is over I am moving to a cottage. Flat country. No stairs at all."

At the eight-hundredth step, on the wide landing called the Widow's Rest, Isolde Varre was waiting for you, in a cloak of dark green, with twenty of her harbour men behind her. Relief went through you like warm water. "Thank all the lamps," Wren gasped. "Isolde, they're right behind us..." Isolde smiled at her, warmly. Then she turned to the Hushed coming up the steps and said, clearly, "Here they are. As agreed." And her men stepped forward, and took your arms.

You will remember Wren's face for the rest of your life. Not anger. Disbelief, and then something worse than anger, a sort of quiet, terrible understanding. They put a hood over your head that smelled of rosemary and river water. You heard Wren shouting, and Hask's roar from far below, cut off. You felt yourself lifted into a cart. You felt it start to move.

And then, in the dark under the hood, very close to your ear, Isolde's voice said softly: "Don't make that face. I can feel you making it. Listen to me. There is exactly one door into the house of the Quiet Order, and it only opens for prisoners, and I have been holding it open for you for ten years." The cart jolted over cobbles. "I have been Calder's eyes inside the Order since you were learning your letters. Your friend will hate me for a week. She'll survive it. Now be quiet and look frightened. You're about to meet the Grand Hush, and he needs to believe he has won."

She lifted the hood an inch, just long enough to press a folded paper into your hand. It was the eighth page of Calder's ledger, and it said: Everyone you trust will be tested. Some will fail. Not all who seem to fail have failed.

## Chapter Nine: The House of False Mirrors

*Escape the Mirror Wards with your memories intact*

The house of the Quiet Order stands on the Mirror Wards, a tangle of narrow streets on the sixth tier where, long ago, the glassmakers of Veyra had their workshops. Its halls are lined with mirrors. Not ordinary mirrors: the Hushed silver them with the grey, so that whoever looks into them sees not their own face but a memory, and not their own memory but one the Order has chosen for them. You were left alone in those halls for three days. The mirrors showed you a childhood you never had. A mother you never knew. A life in which you had never come to Veyra, never met Wren, never held the lantern.

They were very good memories. That was the danger. They were warm and sad and believable, and each one slid in on top of the true ones, the way a new list slides over an old list if you put them in the same place. You did what this month had taught you. You kept your own palace sealed and separate, a route that the mirrors could not reach. Every hour you walked it. Every hour you checked each stop. Every hour, quietly, you named the false memories as false, and set them somewhere else, in a different building, behind a different door.

On the third night, Brother Ennick slipped you out of your cell. "Isolde," he whispered, by way of explanation, and led you down through the dark to the Order's record room: a long, low chamber lined with files, every name in Veyra, every debt, every grief, every secret they had bought or been told. In a locked drawer under the Grand Hush's desk you found a file with a scratched-out face drawn on its cover. Inside was a single sheet. Apprentice-elect to the Archivist, it said. Heir to the Heart. W. Halloway. Hidden by the Archivist's hand. Memory removed by the grey, at her own request. Do not approach until the courier is found.

Wren came for you an hour before dawn, through the drains, with Hask behind her carrying a crowbar the size of an oar. She had not forgiven Isolde. She was not sure she had forgiven you, for some reason she could not put into words. She was soaked to the waist and furious and had never looked more like herself. You put the file in her hands, there in the dark, by the light of the lantern, and watched her read it.

She did not cry. She sat down on the wet stone floor of the drain and read it again, and then again. "The face in the Hall," she said at last. "It was mine. She scratched out my face. She made me drink it and forget it and then she scratched out my face so they wouldn't know who to look for." Her voice cracked. "I thought I was nobody. I thought I was the clerk who couldn't remember anything without a card. And I was... I was her..." She stopped. Hask crouched down beside her, enormous in the narrow tunnel, and put one hand very gently on her shoulder, and said nothing at all, which was exactly right.

Then she stood up and wiped her face on her sleeve and tucked the file inside her coat, in the pocket where she used to keep the notecards. "Right," she said. "Right. I'll fall apart later. I've got it written down." And she nearly laughed. "No. No, I haven't. I'll just have to remember."

You came out of the drains into the river at dawn, a mile below the city, and climbed out onto the bank among the reeds, and lay there in the grey light, breathing. The ninth page of Calder's ledger was in Ennick's pocket; he had taken it off the Grand Hush's desk without knowing what it was. It said: The courier and the heir. One carries the road, the other the way home. Do not let them separate you.

## Chapter Ten: Beyond the Ammerhold

*Travel the Outer Roads and find out who you were*

You could not go back into the city. The Hushed were watching every gate, and posters with your face on them had appeared on the walls, with the words: LOST AND CONFUSED. IF FOUND, BRING TO THE ORDER FOR CARE. So Hask took you over the Ammerhold by the old road, the one the road-wardens use, up through pine woods and over high windy moors where the heather rolled away grey and purple to the edge of the sky, and down into the country of the Outer Roads.

It was beautiful country, green and rolling, full of small grey towns with crooked chimneys and slow brown rivers. And it was sick. In Barrowmere the fields were half-ploughed, the furrows stopping in the middle of the field where someone had simply forgotten what they were doing. In Stillwater the children could not read, and smiled at you, and asked where their mothers had gone, and could not remember that they had asked the same thing an hour before. Everyone was kind. Everyone was calm. Nobody was afraid of anything at all.

In Fenwick Cross you found Tomas Hask. He was mending a fence by the road, slowly and badly, whistling. He looked up at his brother with mild interest and said, "Afternoon. Are you lost? You look lost." Joss Hask stood in the road for a long time. Then he took off his pack, and picked up the other end of the fence rail, and helped his brother mend it, all afternoon, without saying a word. When it was done, Tomas thanked him politely and went inside. Hask stood by the gate until it was dark.

That night, in the old road-wardens' waystation at the crossroads above Fenwick, while Hask sat outside alone, you found the register. It was a fat leather book, every traveller's name and mark for twenty years. You turned the pages idly, by the lantern's light, and then you stopped turning. There, a year ago almost to the day, was an entry in a hand you knew better than any other in the world, because it was your own.

A courier's mark. A name, your name, the Keeper. And a single line: Delivered to the Archivist, Veyra. Returned by choice. Below it, in a different hand, small and fierce, the hand of every ledger page you had found this year: The courier knows the road. Let them forget it. Let them find it again.

You sat with the book open in your lap until the lantern burned low. You had been here before. You had come to Veyra a year ago carrying something for the Archivist. You had left. And you had come back on purpose, knowing, you must have known, what she would ask of you. You did not remember choosing it. But you knew, sitting there in the waystation with the wind in the eaves, that you would have chosen it again.

In the morning Hask was waiting outside, pack on his shoulder, facing the road back toward the city. "Tomas is well fed and safe and doesn't hurt," he said. "That's more than a lot of men get." He looked at the Ammerhold, dark against the sunrise. "There's a man in Veyra who wants to do that to everybody. I'd like to talk to him about it." The tenth page of the ledger was pressed into the back cover of the register. It said: You chose this once. You are allowed to choose it again.

## Chapter Eleven: The Contest of Echoes

*Face the Grand Hush in the Rite of Echoes*

You came back to a city that had begun, slowly, to remember. The lamps you had lit along the Quay were still burning. The portraits still looked down from the Gallery walls. The names were still cut fresh in the Hall of Faces. People had started stopping you in the street to thank you, or to ask you to help them hold on to something: a name, a promise, a recipe, a child's birthday. And Sevrin Ashgrave, the Grand Hush, standing on the steps of the great Amphitheatre with his hood down and the whole city watching, called the Rite of Echoes against the Archive.

By ancient law, any citizen may challenge the keeper of an office to the Rite: a contest of memory before the city. The loser drinks the grey in front of everyone. With Calder gone, the keeper of the Archive was Wren. She went white, and then she went to accept, and you stepped in front of her. The law allows a champion. "Absolutely not," Wren hissed. "You absolutely may not." But you already had, and the crowd had heard, and the Grand Hush smiled at you, sadly, the way a doctor smiles before giving bad news.

It lasted all day. Words, then numbers, then faces, then the old tongue, then the histories of the city. Ten thousand people watched in silence from the great stone tiers. He was very, very good. He had trained in the Art himself as a young man, you realised, long before he ever drank the grey. But he had trained alone, and you had not. Every time you faltered, you looked up and saw Wren in the front row, mouthing the next stop of your route at you, and Hask beside her, and Isolde, who had a great deal of money on the outcome. In the last round, as the sun went down over the Grey Sea, he forgot the name of the first Warden. You did not.

The cup of grey was brought out on a silver tray. Sevrin looked at it for a long moment. Then he pushed it away. "No," he said. "I think not." He turned to the crowd. "You see? Even the Order's own Hush has things he cannot bear to lose. That is the whole of our teaching. That is why it must be done for you, since you will never do it for yourselves." He looked at you. "My sister always said I was too soft for the Art. She was right. It was she who taught me, you know. Elsabet. When we were children."

Before anyone could move, there was a cry from the stands. Old Tansy, the herbalist from the Quay, who had come with a basket of tea to sell, was on her feet, staring at the Grand Hush, her face grey. "Sev," she said, in a voice nobody had ever heard her use. "Sevvy. You've let your beard go. Mother would have a fit." And then she put her hand to her head as if it hurt her, and sat down very suddenly, and looked around her with wide, frightened eyes, as if she did not know where she was.

Sevrin had gone perfectly still. For one moment, the kind face cracked, and underneath it was something raw and young and terrible. Then the mask came back. "The day after tomorrow is the Night of No Moon," he said to the whole Amphitheatre, very quietly, and his voice carried to every tier. "I am going to give you the gift my sister would not. I am going to give you rest." And he walked out through the crowd, and the crowd, from habit, from kindness, from fear, let him go.

Wren was kneeling by Tansy with her arms around her. The old woman was weeping and did not know why. In her basket, under the bundles of rosemary, wrapped in oilcloth, was the eleventh page of the ledger, in the same small, fierce hand as all the others, and it said: If you are reading this, you have found me, and I no longer know you. I am sorry. It was the only safe place left. Look after my brother. He was the kindest of us.

## Chapter Twelve: The Night of No Moon

*Hold the Lethe Gate through the Long Vigil*

The Lethe Gate stands at the head of the city where the river comes roaring out of the gorge: a wall of black stone a hundred feet high, with twelve great iron sluices set in it, each one wider than a house. On the longest night of the year, with no moon in the sky, the river behind it rose and rose until it stood higher than the city roofs, a black mass of water pressing against the iron with a sound like a giant breathing in its sleep. And on top of the Gate, with his hands on the great wheel of the first sluice and a hundred grey-robed Hushed around him, stood Sevrin Ashgrave.

But the city had not stayed home. That was the thing he had not counted on. From every tier of Veyra they came out into the streets with lamps: the fishermen of the Quay, the clerks of the Counting House, the stall-keepers of the Clockwork Market, the families whose names you had cut in the Hall of Faces. For the first time in three hundred years Veyra kept the Long Vigil, and the old songs went up from every street in the dark, ragged and out of tune and glorious. Hask stood at the foot of the Gate stair with Tomas's fence-mending hammer in his fist. Isolde's men held the bridges. And Wren was beside you, as she had been from the first morning.

Sevrin turned the wheel. The first sluice opened with a shriek of iron, and then the second, and the Tide came through. Not a mist. A wall. A great white silent wave of it, rolling down from the Gate over the roofs of the highest tier, and where it passed, the lamps in the windows went out one after another, and the singing stopped.

You did not run. You stood in the middle of the bridge below the Gate with the lantern in your hands, and you closed your eyes, and you began to walk. Not with your feet. In your mind. Along the Quay, past forty-four lamps. Down the Long Gallery, past nine hundred faces. Through the Hall, the Counting House, the Market, the Bridge, the Scriptorium, the Stair, the Mirror Wards, out along the Roads and back, every route you had walked this year, every stop, every picture, joined at last into one great road that ran through all twelve districts of the city. And at the end of it, there was a door you had never seen before, and it opened.

The Heartledger. It had been there all year, the whole of it, waiting at the end of the road you had been building: every true name in Veyra since the founding, every promise of the Compact, every face, every song. Calder had walked it into you on a rainy night a year ago, stop by stop, and then taken away the memory of the walk so that no one could ever force it from you. All you had ever had to do was find your way back. The lantern in your hands blazed up like a sunrise, and far above you, in the dome of the Archive, the Lamp of Ysolde caught fire for the first time in three hundred years.

The Tide stopped on the bridge, a yard from your feet, as if it had come to a wall of glass. And there, in the white of it, lit by the lantern, you found the one memory you had been looking for, because Calder had put it at the very last stop of the road, where she knew you would come at the end: a little girl of six on the Quay steps in the sun, laughing, sailing a paper boat, and a young man with no beard and no grey in his hair, laughing with her. You held it up, the way you would hold up a lamp.

Sevrin saw it. Everyone on the Gate saw it. The Grand Hush let go of the wheel and stood swaying, staring at his daughter's face, and then a sound came out of him like something breaking, and he wept, there on the Gate in front of the whole city, the way he had not let himself weep in twelve years. And then, with his own hands, with the tears running down into his beard, he turned the great wheel back, and the first sluice closed, and the second, and the Tide, cut off from the river, sank down into the streets and thinned and lay there quietly, and was only mist.

Dawn came up grey and gold over the Grey Sea. In the weeks that followed, many things happened. Wren was sworn Archivist in the round hall under the copper dome, with no notecards at all, except one, in her breast pocket, which had your name on it. Hask walked back over the Ammerhold to sit with his brother, and took Brother Ennick with him, and Isolde won a great deal of money from a great many people who had bet against you. Sevrin Ashgrave went to live on the Quay, and sat with Old Tansy every evening under the last lamp, and told her stories about two children she did not remember being.

And Calder, or Tansy, or whoever she was now, came to you one evening with two cups of rosemary tea and asked whether you thought she ought to take back everything she had lost. "I've decided," she said, before you could answer, "to take back only what I need. The rest the river can have. It was always going to take some of it." She sipped her tea. "That's the last lesson, I think. Not how to keep everything. How to choose." She looked at you over the rim of her cup, the way she had looked at you on your very first night on the Quay. "So. Keeper. What will you keep?"

## Epilogue: The Year of Keeping

A year after the Night of No Moon, the city kept the Long Vigil again, and this time nobody had to be asked. On Lamplighters' Quay people gathered in small circles under the lamps to practise remembering together. They passed names and dates around like warm stones from hand to hand. A girl of seven stood on an upturned crate and walked the whole Quay in her head, all forty-four lamps, without a slip, and the fishermen cheered her as if she had landed a whale.

Wren found you by the old stone railing. The Archivist's chain hung crooked round her neck and she had one notecard in her breast pocket, the same one, a little softer at the corners. "Someone changed a date in the eastern ledger," she said. "Three days, on a land sale. I noticed it before I had finished my tea." She looked very pleased with herself and then tried, without much success, to look modest. "I didn't need a card for it. I just knew it was wrong."

A letter came from Joss Hask, carried down from the Ammerhold by a carter who smelled of pine resin and cold wind. The handwriting was jagged and the sentences were short. Tomas sorts buttons by colour in the evenings, he wrote. He does not know me yet. He likes my tea, and he asks my name every morning, and every morning I tell him. It is not nothing. Ennick sends his regards and says to tell you he is still writing his mistakes down. Fewer of them. J. H.

Under the last lamp on the Quay sat Sevrin Ashgrave, with no robe and no beard, holding a cup of rosemary tea in both hands while his sister picked dead leaves off a pot of thyme. She hummed something with no name that she seemed to know all the same. They did not say much. They did not need to. Every evening he told her one story about two children on these steps, and every evening she listened as if it were the first time, and laughed in the same places.

Wren walked you home along the river. "The Tide still comes up, you know," she said. "A little, every night. It always will. Calder says that is not a failure. It is just the river." She stopped at your door. "So we keep walking our routes. A little each day. Not to win anything. Just to keep." Behind you, all the way up the hill to the copper dome, the lamps of Veyra were burning, one for every person who had chosen to remember.

## The Keepers' Circle (closing scene)

The Year of Keeping settled over Veyra like soft wool. The twelve districts stood whole, and you walked the old routes a little each day, with a light step, the way a person walks a street they love.

Wren was waiting at the water's edge as dusk turned the sky violet and gold. "The Tide still leaves a few Forgettings every night," she said. "That is only the river being the river." Along the Quay the Keepers' Circle was gathering: Tansy with her teapot, Fennick with his keys, Isolde, Mosk, Ennick and Hask. Each evening one of them coached and one was coached, and nobody kept score.

Wren put a small brass lamp in your hands, its glass warm against your palm. "The Circle will always have a place for you," she said. "Come when you like. Go when you must. The lamps will be lit either way."
